# OpenAI Python 3.0 makes HTTPX2 an upgrade test for custom clients

Editorial Team

••📖4 min read

![OpenAI Python 3.0 makes HTTPX2 an upgrade test for custom clients](https://magica.com/blog/api/og?title=OpenAI%20Python%203.0%20makes%20HTTPX2%20an%20upgrade%20test%20for%20custom%20clients&seed=openai-python-sdk-httpx2-migration&kind=news&v=4)

OpenAI's Python SDK 3.0.0 replaces httpx with HTTPX2 as its default HTTP client. Standard calls are designed to keep working, but deployments with custom TLS, transports, observability or test integrations need to validate a changed network layer.

* OpenAI Python SDK 3.0.0 defaults to HTTPX2 and no longer installs `httpx` indirectly.
* Default SDK calls retain their documented interface, but the default TLS trust store changes too.
* The practical upgrade work sits with custom clients, test mocks, auth and observability integrations.

OpenAI's official Python library—the generated, typed client for its REST API from Python 3.10 and later—has moved its default HTTP layer from `httpx` to HTTPX2 in version 3.0.0. The package was published on August 11, and the [release notes](https://github.com/openai/openai-python/releases/tag/v3.0.0) classify the switch as breaking: `httpx` is no longer installed automatically.

That does not make every upgrade a rewrite. It makes the transport boundary a deployment test. Applications that use the SDK without a custom HTTP client are documented to retain existing API calls, parsed response models, streaming, authentication, retries and numeric timeouts. But even those applications inherit a different certificate trust store; applications that customize the HTTP layer must migrate the customization itself.

*OpenAI’s v3.0.0 release notes identify the default-client change as a breaking change. [Source: Release v3.0.0 · openai/openai-python · GitHub](https://github.com/openai/openai-python/releases/tag/v3.0.0).*

## Compatible calls, changed TLS assumptions

The [package documentation](https://pypi.org/project/openai/3.0.0/) describes synchronous and asynchronous clients powered by HTTPX2. Its `OpenAI` and `AsyncOpenAI` clients can still be created without an `http_client`, which is the narrow path on which OpenAI says existing behavior continues.

The [migration guide](https://github.com/openai/openai-python/blob/main/httpx2.md) says HTTPX2 uses the operating system's trust store, replacing HTTPX's `certifi` CA bundle, and the SDK no longer installs `certifi`. That can affect minimal container images without system CA certificates, corporate TLS-inspecting proxies and deployments that had relied on a modified `certifi` bundle.

The guide offers explicit certificate-file or certificate-directory configuration, and says those environment settings are honored when , the default. The important distinction is not that every default-client deployment will fail; it is that a network-policy assumption has moved beneath otherwise unchanged SDK calls.

`main`
`# Migrating to HTTPX2
The OpenAI Python SDK now uses [HTTPX2](https://httpx2.pydantic.dev/) for its
synchronous and asynchronous HTTP clients. HTTPX2 is installed automatically
with `openai`; the previous `httpx` package is not. This guide explains what
changes for applications that interact with the SDK's HTTP layer.
## If you use the SDK's default HTTP client
If you construct an `OpenAI` or
`AsyncOpenAI` client without providing `http_client`, your existing API calls,
parsed response models, streaming APIs, authentication, retries, and numeric
timeouts continue to work:
```python
from openai import OpenAI
client = OpenAI(timeout=30.0)
response = client.responses.create(model="gpt-5.5", input="Hello")
````

The main thing is that this transparently will use an OS’s certificate store, not certificates from Python’s `certifi` library module which has certificates sourced from the trust authority of Mozilla.

`certifi`

Answer for yourself: Do you trust an OS vendor or the OS certificate installation mechanism more than Python supply chain to not perform man-in-the-middle on OpenAI API https requests?

Also, this breaks compatibility with Python 3.9 and before - dashing any hopes of running on Windows 7 or some default Linux installs, the last Python version there, but with new auth components provided by Python.
